Angle mort : un jeu de cartes pour récon: Angle mort: a card game to reconnect racialized high school students with history

Il y a plus d’un an, je me rendais dans: More than a year ago, I visited the offices of Philo-Boxe. Karim Coppry, the organization's founder, was sitting with a group of teachers, brainstorming a card game meant to improve the relationship between students and teachers.
Un an plus tard, le projet prend vie : A: A year later, the project has come to life: Angle mort. This 52-card game explores the history of racialized communities. It aims to spark reflection in schools, include these communities in the narrative, strengthen students' sense of belonging and, in turn, improve their relationships with their teachers.
Vendredi, j’ai assisté au lancement d’An: On Friday, Maïssem and I attended the launch of Angle mort. Young people got to discover the card game alongside teachers and curious onlookers.
Je vous laisse, à votre tour, découvrir: Now it's your turn to discover this initiative!
<strong>Lorsque des élèves du secondaire: When high school students don't see themselves in what they're taught, how can we nurture their sense of belonging and keep them from dropping out? Angle mort, an educational card game created by Philo-Boxe and Exeko, tackles this question by bringing to life the erased histories of Quebec's racialized communities.
<strong>Mardi 26 août, 17 h, au Chalet K: Tuesday, August 26, 5 p.m., at Chalet Kent in Côte-des-Neiges. With its high wooden ceilings, a ping-pong table in the middle of the room and a few teenagers absorbed in a PlayStation a little farther off, the youth centre lives up to its name. The smell of Haitian food mingles with that of a Lebanese dish. The plates, like the room, reflect a multiethnic Montréal.
C’est ici que se tient la première prése: This is where Angle mort is being presented for the first time. The educational card game is designed to enrich the teaching of history in high school by making sure students feel seen and heard in the stories told at school. Two teams quickly form around the ping-pong table. The high school students take centre stage, while curious adults join in.
Christine Chevalier-Caron, professeure d: Christine Chevalier-Caron, a CEGEP history teacher and co-author of the game, asks the first question: “How does the Sir George Williams affair show that access to education was marked by multiple inequalities for certain populations?”
Silence dans la salle. Quelques visages: Silence in the room. A few faces tense up, until a hesitant voice speaks up: “Is it about the Guy-Concordia story?”
Une participante raconte comment, à la f: One participant explains how, in the late 1960s, Black students denounced a biology professor accused of failing students from their community to keep them out of the medical program. M<sup>s</sup> Chevalier-Caron fills in the rest of the story. Around the table, faces light up. People are discovering, learning.
<strong>Renforcer les liens entre profs: Strengthening ties between teachers and students by recognizing the history of racialized communities
Si, ce soir, des adolescents découvrent: If teenagers are discovering little-known chapters of Quebec history tonight, it's thanks to Karim Coppry, the founder of Philo-Boxe. He isn't a teacher, but he spends his days with the young people he trains. What often comes up in his conversations with them is the discomfort students feel not only about history class, but also about their teachers.
« Avec ce jeu-là, notre objectif était v: “With this game, our goal was really to improve teacher-student relationships. At first, we thought of a more relational game, with discussions and themes, but it was too complicated. So we went back to a simple format: questions and answers based on the official curriculum, but with angles that aren't discussed in Quebec's school system,” the founder says. “We wanted to create a tool that also offers possibilities for teachers. So they don't feel like they're just ‘getting through the material,’ but feel involved in a dialogue with students,” Karim continues.
Pour lui, il s’agit là du véritable enje: For him, this is the real issue: that bond between teachers and students still needs to be built. “Teachers are significant people for young people. Kids really spend 90% of their time with them. So it's important for schools to have that space for dialogue and that space for recognizing one another. That bond could also help keep young people from dropping out, and even [encourage] them to stay in school,” he believes.
Il ajoute que les cours d’histoire etde: He adds that history classes and Quebec Culture and Citizenship classes play a decisive role in students' education. But what happens when a student finds no points of reference in the collective story? “Obviously it's harder. It's hard to feel like you're part of society. That's why it's important to include diverse points of reference, the struggles and recent contributions of certain communities, so that every community can see itself in the education system,” Karim insists.
Il cite notamment l’histoire du jazz, po: He points in particular to the history of jazz, carried by Caribbean communities in Montréal: “The city was a hub, but at school, it's barely mentioned. The result: only people who know the history of Little Burgundy have access to it. And yet it's a legitimate source of pride for these communities: showing that they're not confined to certain clichés, but that they've contributed something to Quebec and Canadian society.”
<strong>« On ne nous explique pas ce qu’: “They don't explain to us what really happened [in history]”
Alors que le jeu prend fin, quelques ado: As the game wraps up, a few teenagers hang back at the chalet. The conversation drifts to how history is taught to them. Amid laughter and horsing around, one thing becomes clear: many of them, who come from immigrant backgrounds, say they feel a lack of belonging.
Ines, d’origine marocaine, est en 4<sup>: Ines, who is of Moroccan origin, is in her 4<sup>th</sup> year of high school. She confides: “In 1<sup>st</sup>, 2<sup>nd</sup> and 3<sup>rd </sup>year, we never talked about my community in history. When I'm in history class, it can interest me, but I don't feel like it's about me. It only talks about Quebecers… I'm a Quebecer, but I don't feel like a Quebecer,” she admits.
Elle regrette que la matière ne reflète: She regrets that the subject doesn't reflect Quebec's real diversity. “It's too bad, because history is the only class where we really talk about societies. We should talk about every community, or no one,” she says flatly.
Même constat pour Zacharias, qui aura bi: Zacharias, who is about to turn 18 and just got his high school diploma, feels the same way. “Me, I found history classes all over the place… It didn't interest me, it bored me. Teachers talking the whole time…” he says. When asked whether a more playful approach would change how he feels about the subject, he answers enthusiastically. “Obviously! Actually, I had one teacher who helped me pass my exam because he'd ask just one question at the start of class, and then we had to discuss, participate,” he recalls.
Pour le jeune homme, un jeu comme Angle: For the young man, a game like Angle mort is much more relevant. “For sure I'd like us to talk about all the communities that have contributed to society in Quebec. That would interest me more than hearing over and over that Quebecers came and stole from Indigenous people. We don't talk about Jews, we talk about Indigenous people, [we talk] about Black people real quick, and on top of that, they don't explain to us what really happened. When we talk about Indigenous people, they don't teach us about the Church's role in the massacres, for example,” he says.
<strong>Contrer les discours actuels sur: Countering today's discourse on immigration through history
Pour la professeure d'histoire Christine: For history teacher Christine Chevalier-Caron, the problem is clear: the history being taught is told from a Eurocentric point of view and through a nationalist lens rooted in French Canada. As a result, it gives the impression that immigration is a recent phenomenon, limited to the 1980s. “And yet most of the profiles of people here in Quebec have been present since the 18<sup>th</sup> or 19<sup>th</sup> century,” she points out.
C’est cette profondeur historique que l’: It's precisely this historical depth that the teacher wants to bring to light. She gives a telling example: the Haitian community, which arrived in large numbers in the 1960s. “Many were fleeing the Duvalier regime. They were doctors, teachers, professionals who contributed directly to the Quiet Revolution. At the time, there were very few francophone Québécois doctors or lawyers,” she says.
L’arrivée de la communauté haïtienne a é: The arrival of the Haitian community was a turning point in the history of contemporary Quebec, the teacher continues. “But that's not what you see in history textbooks. Knowing that would allow [Haitian students] to realize, ‘We built the health-care system, you know!’”
Selon M<sup>me</sup> Chevalier-Caron, ce: According to M<sup>s</sup> Chevalier-Caron, this knowledge would help counter the narrative that presents immigration as a recent phenomenon and show students from immigrant backgrounds that they are not mere “newcomers,” but have long been an integral part of the social fabric.
« En fait, il y a de grosses lacunes dan: “In fact, there are huge gaps in how history is taught,” the teacher stresses, deploring both the government's inaction on the issue and an inadequate curriculum.
L’enseignante n’en est pas à ses premièr: This isn't the first time the teacher has thought about how to make history class more inclusive. She has already worked on textbooks and has often been forced to leave these stories out. With Angle mort, she can finally bring them back into the spotlight.
M<sup>me</sup> Chevalier-Caron est cepen: M<sup>s</sup> Chevalier-Caron is aware, however, that any change in how history is taught draws mixed reactions, and that Angle mort won't be received the same way everywhere. She recalls in particular the outcry in 2018, when all textbooks were pulled from classrooms so the term “Amerindians” could be replaced with “First Nations” or “Indigenous.” “Half the teachers welcomed this progress, but the other half said, ‘You're changing our history, you just want to sweep it away, it's historical revisionism!’” she says, noting the influence of very powerful lobbies. In an amused tone, she concludes: “I think there are places where we'll be really well received, and others where they'll scream, accuse us of sabotaging Quebec's national history.”
Mais pour les étudiants, les effets pour: But for students, the effects could be decisive. “Those who don't see themselves at all in the school narrative will finally see [that] their history [is being taken into account]. That creates pride, a sense of belonging,” the teacher believes. And for Quebec's white majority, she adds, “it can shed light on facts, help break down certain stereotypes, add nuance to political or media discourse on immigration.” “It's a way to create a real intercultural exchange, to bring groups closer together, to see what we have in common, and to be more sensitive to the historical injustices some groups have experienced and still experience today,” she continues.
Face à ces constats d’exclusion et de dé: Faced with this exclusion and lack of interest, some teachers are trying to reinvent the way history is taught. That's what Sarah*, a history teacher at a Montréal high school, is trying to do. With a colourful scarf tied around her head, gold jewellery and purple mascara, she embodies the freshness and boldness of this new way of teaching.
« J’ai la chance et le privilège de veni: “I have the luck and the privilege of coming from an anti-racist activist community in Montréal. So I was already aware of how history is made and why it's told one way or another. For me, it was important to decentre, to decolonize the content I was presenting to students…” the teacher says.
Pour Sarah, l’histoire est une science,: For Sarah, history is a science, and every teacher can choose their angle of analysis, whether feminist, decolonial or otherwise. “But you already need to have that knowledge and be sensitive to those approaches. I have a lot of Haitian students in my classes: it's not in the curriculum, but I talk about the Haitian Revolution, and it makes them proud to see that their history matters, just like the history of the 19th and 20th centuries,” she explains.
La professeure reconnaît néanmoins que c: The teacher acknowledges, however, that this kind of teaching requires time and skills that not every teacher necessarily has. “Our workload is heavy and sometimes we don't have time to look for other resources,” she laments.
C’est justement en pensant à cette réali: It's precisely with this reality in mind that Angle mort was designed: as a tool that serves students as much as teachers, without adding to the workload. A bet that seems to have paid off for Sarah: “Now, with a turnkey product, there are no more excuses,” she says with a quiet laugh.
Au cours des prochains mois, Karim et Ch: In the coming months, Karim and Christine want to expand the project, build partnerships with schools across the Greater Montréal area, train teachers to use it and get Angle mort into more classrooms. Coming soon to a classroom near you!
